app.title: Lactomeda — Mission Control
app.tagline: Design a space mission, then keep it alive.

scenario.heading: Choose your mission
scenario.intro: Each mission has its own goal, budget and deadline. There is no single right answer. Pick one to start.

placeholder.hint: Walk with WASD, press E at a station.

requirements.heading: Set your targets
requirements.intro: Turn the goals of {{name}} into numbers you will be scored on. Harder targets earn more points but are harder to build.

levelHelp.threshold: The least you can accept. Miss this and the goal fails.
levelHelp.baseline: What the mission promises. A balanced choice.
levelHelp.goal: The stretch target. Best science, hardest to build.

requirements.potentialHelp: The average of your levels. It boosts the goals part of your final score.
requirements.pressureNone: Nothing above baseline: an easy, balanced start.

payload.heading: Pick your instruments
payload.intro: Instruments collect the science. Each one adds weight, power use, cost and data that the spacecraft must handle.
payload.noBus: You have not picked a spacecraft size yet. Slot limits will apply once you do.
payload.slotsFull: No free slot on this bus. Remove an instrument or pick a bigger bus.
payload.helpsNone: Not needed for this mission’s goals

incompatible.objective: Measures nothing this mission needs. The mission needs: {{needs}}.
incompatible.orbit: Only works from {{orbits}}, and this mission can’t fly there.
incompatible.chosenOrbit: Doesn’t work from your chosen orbit ({{orbit}}).
incompatible.title: Not available

payload.marginal_one: +{{value}} science (half, because you already have one)

orbit.heading: Choose your orbit
orbit.intro: Your orbit decides how sharp your images are, how long you sit in shadow, how often you can talk to the ground, and how much radiation you get.
orbit.notAllowed: This mission can’t fly here. The scenario doesn’t allow this orbit.

leo.goodFor: Sharp Earth images and low-cost missions close to home.
leo.tradeoff: Short chances to talk to the ground. Thin air slowly pulls the spacecraft down.

sso.goodFor: Earth observation with the same lighting every day.
sso.tradeoff: Needs a more powerful launch than a plain low orbit.

meo.tradeoff: Strong radiation from the Van Allen belts.

geo.goodFor: Weather and nonstop watch over one region.
geo.tradeoff: Less detailed images, an expensive launch, and a long way to send data.

molniya.goodFor: Long views of the far north.
molniya.tradeoff: Crosses the radiation belts twice a day.

l2.goodFor: Telescopes: stable, cold, with the Sun always behind.
l2.tradeoff: Needs NASA’s Deep Space Network, and data comes home slowly.

lunar.tradeoff: Takes lots of fuel to reach, and Earth is far away.

mars.goodFor: Mars science and relaying rover data.
mars.tradeoff: Sunlight is only 43% as strong as at Earth, and the trip takes months.

orbit.confirmNeeds: Pick an orbit, a rocket and ground stations to continue.

launcher.heading: Choose your launcher
launcher.intro: The rocket must lift your spacecraft to your orbit. Bigger rockets lift more and go farther, but cost more. Cheap rides can be riskier.
launcher.pickOrbitFirst: Pick an orbit above to see which launchers can reach it.

ground.heading: Choose your ground stations
ground.intro: Your spacecraft can only send data home when a ground station can see it. More and bigger stations mean more minutes per day, but they cost more each year.
ground.contact: Time to send data home each day
ground.pickOrbit: Pick an orbit to see the minutes
ground.tooFar: Too far: reaches up to {{reach}}, your orbit is {{distance}} away.

catalog.gn-university: One small dish on campus. Cheap, but it only sees you a few times a day.
catalog.gn-commercial: A rented network of stations around the world: many more chances per day.
catalog.gn-nen: NASA’s network for spacecraft near Earth, as far as the Moon and L2.
catalog.gn-dsn: NASA’s giant dishes in California, Spain and Australia. The only way to reach deep space.

cml.heading: Mission progress
cml.debriefNone: Your concept has not reached CML 1 yet.
cml.help: (NASA/JPL Concept Maturity Level) NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory rates how developed a mission idea is, from CML 1 to 4. Each phase of the game moves your idea up one level.

segments.heading: The 4 parts of every mission
segments.help: NASA splits every science mission into four parts: launch, space, ground and user.
segments.summaryIntro: Your design so far, sorted the way NASA plans a science mission.

line.contact: Time to send data home each day

users.student-cubesat: Your university team, space-weather researchers and radio amateurs who listen to your CubeSat.
users.wildfire-eo: Firefighters and emergency agencies, who use fresh fire maps to decide where to send crews.
users.space-telescope: Astronomers around the world, who request observing time and download the data from public archives.

bus.heading: Build your spacecraft
bus.intro: The bus is the spacecraft around your instruments: its frame, power, computer and radio. Bigger buses carry more, but cost more and need bigger rockets.
bus.partsHeading: 2. Pick one part for each subsystem
bus.trlHelp: TRL (Technology Readiness Level) shows how proven a part is. 9 = flown many times. Lower = newer and riskier.
bus.confirmNeeds: Choose a bus size and a part for every subsystem to continue.

structure.name: Structure
structure.what: The frame that holds everything together.

power.name: Power
power.what: Makes electricity: solar panels, or an RTG far from the Sun.

battery.name: Battery
battery.what: Keeps everything running while the spacecraft is in shadow.

computer.name: Computer
computer.what: Runs the spacecraft and stores data until it can be sent home.

attitude.name: Pointing
attitude.what: Attitude control keeps the spacecraft facing the right way: cameras at the target, antennas at Earth.

propulsion.name: Propulsion
propulsion.what: Thrusters to change orbit, dodge junk and stay up longer.

thermal.name: Thermal
thermal.what: Keeps parts from getting too hot or too cold.

comms.name: Comms
comms.what: The radio that sends your data to the ground stations.

issues.UNKNOWN_COMPONENT: A part for {{subsystem}} no longer exists: pick another one.
issues.WRONG_SUBSYSTEM: That part does not belong to {{subsystem}}: pick another one.
issues.LOW_SOLAR_POWER: Far from the Sun, solar panels make much less power. Consider an RTG.
issues.TOO_MANY_INSTRUMENTS: Too many instruments for this bus: remove one or pick a bigger bus.
issues.TOO_MANY_COMPONENTS: Too many parts for this bus (backups count twice). Pick a bigger bus.
issues.OVER_BUS_MASS: Too heavy for this bus: pick a bigger bus or lighter parts.
issues.UNKNOWN_BUS_CLASS: This bus size no longer exists: pick another one.

landing.tagline: Design a NASA-style space mission, then keep it alive.

hint.solo: Plan and fly a mission on your own.

howTo.heading: How to play
howTo.design: Design: pick a mission and set its targets. Then build the spacecraft and choose instruments, orbit, rocket and ground stations.
howTo.resources: Watch the resource bar: weight, power, budget, data, radio and time. Green is fine, amber is tight, red is over.
howTo.maturity: Each finished phase raises your mission progress, the way NASA JPL rates real mission ideas (CML 1 to 4).
howTo.flight: Fly: walk around your ship and fix emergencies at each station before time runs out.
howTo.debrief: Debrief: see your score and why the mission worked or failed. Then fly again with one change.

landing.sourcesHint: The NASA resources behind this game.
landing.offlineReason: The team server can’t be reached right now. Play Solo still works.

items.mass: Everything the spacecraft weighs: parts, instruments and fuel. It must fit the bus limit and what the rocket can lift to your orbit.
items.power: The electricity the spacecraft uses, compared with what its solar panels or RTG make. In shadow there is no sunlight, so no solar power.
items.budget: Money for the whole mission: building the spacecraft, the launch and paying ground stations every year until the mission ends.
items.data: Science data your instruments collect each day, compared with how much you can send to Earth. Data you can’t send is lost.
items.comms: Minutes per day you need to talk to Earth, compared with the minutes ground stations can actually see your spacecraft.
items.time: How long the mission must last, compared with how long the spacecraft will probably survive. Radiation and weak parts shorten its life.
items.cubesat-1u: A 10 cm cube, about 1 kg. The smallest standard satellite: room for one tiny instrument. Great for learning, very cheap.
items.cubesat-2u: Two 1U cubes stacked: 20 cm long. A little more room for batteries or a slightly bigger instrument.
items.cubesat-3u: Three cubes, the size of a loaf of bread. The most popular CubeSat: enough room for two small instruments.
items.cubesat-6u: Two 3U CubeSats side by side. Room for bigger solar panels, better pointing and small thrusters.
items.cubesat-12u: The biggest common CubeSat, like a small suitcase. Can carry three instruments and serious power.
items.smallsat: A satellite up to about 180 kg that rides on the ESPA ring under a bigger payload. Real science missions fit here.
items.medium: A spacecraft up to 1.5 tonnes, like many weather and Earth-science satellites. Needs its own medium rocket.
items.large: A flagship spacecraft up to 6.5 tonnes, like big NASA observatories. Carries many instruments, costs hundreds of millions.
items.str-3u: An aluminium frame made to the CubeSat standard so it fits any CubeSat deployer.
items.str-12u: A larger CubeSat frame with rails that slide into a 12U deployer.
items.str-smallsat: A metal box built to the ESPA standard, the ring that carries small satellites on big rockets.
items.str-large: A strong aluminium structure for a big spacecraft. Heavy, but well tested on many missions.
items.str-composite: Carbon-fibre panels: much lighter than aluminium for the same strength, but newer and more expensive.
items.pwr-body: Solar cells glued on the outside of the spacecraft. Simple and reliable, but small, so they make little power.
items.pwr-deploy: Solar panels that unfold like wings after launch. Much more power for a CubeSat, with a small risk they don’t open.
items.pwr-array-small: Folding solar wings for a SmallSat, making hundreds of watts in sunlight.
items.pwr-array-large: Huge solar wings for big spacecraft, making thousands of watts. Heavy and expensive.
items.pwr-rtg: Makes electricity from the heat of decaying plutonium, like the Curiosity rover. Works far from the Sun and in darkness. Very expensive.
items.bat-40: A small lithium-ion pack, like a few phone batteries. Keeps a CubeSat alive while it passes through Earth’s shadow.
items.bat-1k: A 1 kWh lithium-ion battery for SmallSats: enough to run instruments through each shadow pass.
items.bat-10k: A big battery bank for large spacecraft that use a lot of power in shadow.
items.bat-adv: A new high-density battery: stores more energy for its weight, but hasn’t flown as often.
items.obc-cubesat: A small, cheap computer built from normal electronics. Works well in low orbit but radiation can glitch it.
items.obc-radtol: A computer designed to tolerate radiation: fewer glitches during solar storms and in higher orbits.
items.obc-radhard: A radiation-hardened computer like the RAD750 used on Mars rovers. Very reliable, slow and expensive.
items.obc-edge: A powerful computer that processes images on board and sends only the useful parts. New technology, less tested.
items.adcs-mag: Coils that push against Earth’s magnetic field to turn the spacecraft. Light and cheap, but not very precise.
items.adcs-cubesat: Tiny spinning wheels plus a star camera: points a CubeSat accurately enough for imaging.
items.adcs-smallsat: Reaction wheels and star trackers: precise pointing for SmallSat cameras and antennas.
items.adcs-cmg: Control moment gyroscopes: big spinning wheels that can turn large spacecraft quickly, like the ISS uses.
items.adcs-fine: An extra-precise pointing system that keeps a telescope locked on a star, like Hubble or JWST.
items.prop-none: No engine at all. Lighter and cheaper, but the spacecraft cannot change orbit or dodge debris.
items.prop-coldgas: Small puffs of compressed gas. Gentle and safe, enough for small corrections on a CubeSat.
items.prop-mono: Hydrazine thrusters, used on most satellites to stay in orbit and dodge junk for years.
items.prop-biprop: A main engine burning two propellants: powerful enough to reach the Moon or Mars orbit. Very heavy.
items.prop-hall: An electric thruster that pushes charged gas with magnets. Tiny push but very efficient; needs lots of power.
items.thm-passive: Special paint and gold blankets (MLI) that keep the spacecraft at a safe temperature with no power.
items.thm-heaters: Insulating blankets plus small electric heaters that turn on when parts get too cold.
items.thm-radiators: Pumps move heat to radiator panels that shed it to space. Needed for powerful, hot instruments.
items.thm-cryo: A sunshield and cryocooler that keep a telescope extremely cold, like JWST, so it can see infrared light.
items.com-uhf: A simple radio that amateur stations can hear. Very slow: a few kilobits per second (kbps).
items.com-sband: A common satellite radio with a flat antenna. About 100 times faster than UHF.
items.com-xband: A fast radio used by Earth-observation satellites to send down huge images during short passes.
items.com-hga: A big dish antenna that can talk across millions of kilometres to NASA’s Deep Space Network.
items.com-optical: Sends data with a laser instead of radio: extremely fast, but must point very precisely. Newer technology.
items.inst-visible-cam: A small camera that takes colour pictures of Earth, like a phone camera with a telephoto lens.
items.inst-multispectral: Takes pictures in many colours of light, including some we can’t see. Shows plants, water, burn scars and smoke.
items.inst-thermal-ir: Sees heat instead of light. Spots active fires, even through smoke and at night.
items.inst-sar: A radar that makes its own images by bouncing radio waves off the ground. Sees through clouds, day and night.
items.inst-spectrometer: Splits light into a rainbow to find out what something is made of, like gases in a planet’s air.
items.inst-magnetometer: Measures magnetic fields, to study Earth’s magnetism and space weather.
items.inst-telescope: A large mirror that collects faint light from far-away galaxies and planets. Heavy, precise and very expensive.
items.inst-laser-alt: Fires laser pulses at the ground and times their return to map heights, like the shape of the Moon’s surface.
items.inst-particle: Counts charged particles from the Sun and space, to measure radiation and space weather.
items.inst-radiometer: Measures microwaves coming from Earth to learn about rain, moisture and temperature in the air.
items.inst-magnetometer-cubesat: A tiny magnetometer on a short boom, small enough for a student CubeSat.
items.leo: Low Earth Orbit, 500 km up: one lap every 95 minutes. Close for sharp images, but contact with the ground is short and air drag slowly lowers it.
items.sso: A polar orbit timed so the spacecraft passes over each place at the same local time every day: same lighting for every picture.
items.meo: About 20,000 km up, where GPS satellites fly. One lap every 12 hours, inside strong radiation belts.
items.geo: 36,000 km above the equator: one lap per day, so the satellite seems to stand still over one region. Used for weather.
items.molniya: A long, stretched orbit that hangs high over the far north for hours, then swoops low. Used for polar coverage.
items.l2: A balance point 1.5 million km from Earth, always on the night side. The Sun, Earth and Moon stay behind the telescope.
items.lunar: A low orbit 100 km above the Moon, for mapping its surface. Reaching it takes a lot of fuel.
items.mars: A low orbit around Mars, months of travel away. Sunlight is weaker there and messages take minutes to arrive.
items.lv-csli: NASA’s CubeSat Launch Initiative gives free rides to selected student and education CubeSats.
items.lv-cubesat: Your CubeSat rides in a spring-loaded box and is pushed out from the ISS or another rocket. Cheap, but low orbit only.
items.lv-rideshare: Share a big rocket with dozens of other satellites, like SpaceX Transporter flights. Cheap, but you go where they go.
items.lv-small: A small dedicated rocket like Rocket Lab’s Electron: your satellite chooses the orbit and launch date.
items.lv-medium: A reusable medium rocket like Falcon 9. Can reach high orbits, the Moon and beyond for medium spacecraft.
items.lv-heavy: A heavy rocket like Falcon Heavy or Ariane 6 for big spacecraft or deep-space missions.
items.lv-superheavy: NASA’s Space Launch System class: the most powerful rocket, for the heaviest missions to the Moon and beyond.
items.gn-university: One small antenna on a university roof. It only sees your satellite for a few short passes a day.
items.gn-commercial: Rent time on antennas around the world, so your satellite is in contact many more times per day.
items.gn-nen: NASA’s Near Space Network: antennas and relay satellites for missions near Earth, out to the Moon.
items.gn-dsn: NASA’s Deep Space Network: giant 34–70 m dishes in California, Spain and Australia that talk to spacecraft across the solar system.

difficultyPicker.heading: Choose a difficulty
difficultyPicker.intro: Harder levels unlock advanced parts, but bring more emergencies and less room to spare.

who.flightDirector: Little room to spare, lots of trouble.

difficultyPicker.riskNo: Every red must be fixed before launch
difficultyPicker.riskYes: Can launch by accepting the risk

altitude.heading: Fine-tune the altitude
altitude.intro: Lower gives sharper images, but thin air drags the spacecraft down sooner. Higher lasts longer but sees less detail.
altitude.label: Altitude
altitude.noImager: Add a camera or imager on the Payload screen to see its image detail here.

limitedBy.propellant: ends when fuel for staying up runs out
limitedBy.orbitDecay: ends when the orbit sinks too low

flight.flyAgainHelp: Your design is kept. Change one thing, fly again and compare.
flight.sameEvents: Same launch roll and emergencies as last time, so only your changes matter.
flight.newEvents: Same design, but the launch roll and emergencies are drawn again.
flight.noChanges: Nothing changed yet. Change one thing and fly again to see its effect.

sources.heading: NASA Sources
sources.intro: This game uses the {{count}} resources of the NASA Space Apps challenge. Each one has a job in the game. Here is what it does and where you see it.
sources.alsoFromNasa: Also from NASA: the real missions in the debrief comparison (Landsat 9, GOES-R, JWST, LRO, MRO) come from NASA mission pages. NASA images are credited where they are used.

scienceMissions.name: Design and Develop Science Missions
scienceMissions.use: The four mission parts (launch, space, ground and user) organise the design tabs and the report. The user part shows who uses your data, like fire agencies in the wildfire mission.

gmat.name: GMAT (General Mission Analysis Tool)
gmat.use: We computed our orbits with NASA GMAT scripts: orbit time, time in Earth’s shadow and minutes of ground contact per day. The power and radio budgets use those numbers.
gmat.where: Orbit cards ("computed with NASA GMAT"), power and comms budgets

cml.name: Concept Maturity Levels (JPL)
cml.use: The design phases follow JPL’s maturity levels, CML 1 to 4. The progress meter rises as your concept grows, and the debrief shows the level you reached.

mdl.name: Mission Design Lab (NASA Goddard)
mdl.use: The design review works like a Mission Design Lab study: one finding per subject, plus an equipment list and cost. Those subjects are also the rooms of your ship.
mdl.where: Design review, ship rooms, mission report

missionViz.name: NASA Mission Viz
missionViz.use: The debrief opens a real mission like yours, and its trajectory views inspire our launch and orbit animation.
missionViz.where: Debrief ("See a real mission like yours")

telescopeGame.name: A Learning Game About Telescopes
telescopeGame.use: Your goal decides which kind of light you observe, and that decides which instruments fit. Parts that don’t fit are greyed out, with the reason.
telescopeGame.where: Payload screen, Space Telescope mission, debrief

cubesat101.name: CubeSat 101 (NASA CubeSat Launch Initiative)
cubesat101.use: The Student CubeSat mission follows it: unit sizes, how a CubeSat gets a launch, licences and typical part values.

vrChallenge.name: Visualize a Space Mission Using VR (Space Apps 2023)
vrChallenge.use: Its concept → trajectory → timeline structure shapes the timeline of the flight HUD.

csaGames.name: Digital games and activities (Canadian Space Agency)
csaGames.use: Our model for simple, friendly explanations. Canada’s RADARSAT radar satellites inspire the radar instrument.

review.heading: Design review
review.intro: Like a study at NASA’s Mission Design Lab, each subject checks your design before launch. Fix the red items, or accept the risk if your difficulty allows it.

overall.go: Every check passed: ready to launch.
overall.concern: You can launch, but some margins are tight.
overall.noGo: Something must be fixed before launch.

review.acceptRisk: I accept the risk: launch even with red items. The mission is more likely to fail.

decision.clear: Design review passed. Ready to launch.
decision.hardBlockers: Something essential is missing. Fix the red items first.
decision.riskNotAccepted: Some items are red. Fix them, or accept the risk to launch.
decision.cadetCannotAcceptRisk: On Cadet you can't launch with red items. Fix them first.
